ety.text: From Middle English mone, from Old English mōna (“moon”), from Proto-West Germanic *mānō, from Proto-Germanic *mēnô (“moon”), from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon; month”), probably from *meh₁- (“to measure”).

senses.d: Any natural satellite of a planet.
ex: The stargazer observed the moons of Jupiter for over a year.
That's no moon, you idiot... it's a space station!

senses.d: A month, particularly a lunar month.
ex: They stayed with their aunt and uncle for many moons.

senses.d: A representation of the moon, usually as a crescent or as a circle with a face; a crescent-shaped shape, symbol, or object.
ex: The wizard costume was decorated with stars and moons.

senses.d: A crescent-like outwork in a fortification.
ex: The moons surrounding the city walls were built in the sixteenth century.

senses.d: The eighteenth trump/major arcana card of the tarot.
The thirty-second Lenormand card.
In hearts, the action of taking all the point cards in one hand.
To display one's buttocks to, typically as a jest, insult, or protest.
ex: The hooligans mooned the riot police.
It was ill-advised of Sam to moon the photographer during the shoot.

senses.d: To gaze at lovingly or in adoration.
ex: To completely back down now would be as unnatural as mooning in front of your girlfriend's parents.

senses.d: To fuss over something adoringly; to be infatuated with someone.
ex: Sarah mooned over Sam's photograph for months.
You've been mooning after her forever; why not just ask her out?

senses.d: To spend time idly, absent-mindedly.
ex: We were only three on board. The poor old skipper mooned in the cabin.
I mooned around. I was mighty sick of the room by then.

senses.d: To expose to the rays of the Moon.
To adorn with moons or crescents.
To rise in price rapidly or suddenly. (from to the moon)
ex: It is impractical if a currency moons and plummets often.

senses.d: To shoot the moon.

grp.label: the natural satellite of planet Earth
any substantially sized natural satellite of a planet

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French lune, from Old French lune, from Latin lūna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, from *lewk- + *-sneh₂.

From Luna, from Latin lūna, from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include Armenian լուսին (lusin), Spanish luna, Portuguese lua, Romanian lună, Russian луна́ (luná).
Inherited from Old Spanish luna, from Latin lūna. Cognate with Asturian lluna, Catalan lluna, French lune, Galician lúa, Italian luna, Occitan luna, Portuguese lua, and Romanian lună.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lũa, from Latin lūna (“moon”), from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, which is derived from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-. Cognate with Galician lúa, Spanish, Italian, and Occitan luna, Catalan lluna, French lune, and Romanian lună.

Inherited from Middle French moys, from Old French mois, from earlier meis, from Latin mēnsis. Compare Catalan mes, Italian mese, Occitan mes, Portuguese mês, Romansh mais, Spanish mes.
From Latin mēnsem (“month”). Compare Catalan mes, French mois, Portuguese mês, Romansh mais, Spanish mes.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mes, from Latin mēnsis (“month”). Compare Galician, Spanish, and Catalan mes, Italian mese, French mois, and Romansh mais.

Earlier mus, moos, from an Eastern Algonquian language name for the animal, such as Massachusett moos, mws, Narragansett moos or Penobscot mos (cognate to Abenaki moz), from Proto-Algonquian *mo·swa (“it strips”), referring to how a moose strips tree bark when feeding: compare Massachusett moos-u (“he strips, cuts smooth”).
Borrowed from Japanese むすめ (“daughter”).

senses.d: The largest member of the deer family (Alces americanus, sometimes included in Alces alces), of which the male has very large, palmate antlers.
ex: We saw a moose at the edge of the woods.

senses.d: Any of the extinct moose-like deer of the genera Cervalces and Libralces.
ex: Europe’s giant beavers lived at the same time as the first moose, Libralces gallicus.

senses.d: An ugly person.
An Asian girl taken as a lover.
ex: In military bases in the rear areas it was common for soldiers to have a moose.

From Middle English mood, mode, mod, from Old English mōd (“mind,” in poetry also “heart, spirit, courage”), from Proto-West Germanic *mōd, from Proto-Germanic *mōdaz (“sense, courage, zeal, anger”), from Proto-Indo-European *moh₁-, *meh₁- (“endeavour, will, temper”).
Alteration of mode, from Latin modus, with specialized uses in grammar, music and logic.

senses.d: A mental or emotional state, composure.
ex: I've been in a bad mood since I was dumped by my ex-boyfriend.

I envy not in any moods
⁠The captive void of noble rage,
⁠The linnet born within the cage,
That never knew the summer woods: […]

senses.d: Emotional character (of a work of music, literature, or other art).
A sullen, gloomy or angry mental state; a bad mood.
ex: He's in a mood with me today.
He was beginning to forget his burdening, despairing mood of a short while ago.

senses.d: A disposition to do something, a state of mind receptive or disposed to do something.
ex: I'm not in the mood for running today.
"The Placer SPCA brings by some kittens and puppies, and I do my best to get everyone tipsy and in a donating mood."

senses.d: A prevalent atmosphere, attitude, or feeling.
ex: A good politician senses the mood of the crowd.
A novel that catches the mood of prewar Berlin.

senses.d: A familiar, relatable feeling, experience, or thing.
ex: “I'm only here for a night. I'm road tripping with a friend and he decided we needed a queer bar, stat.” “Oh, that's a whole mood.”
To borrow an idiom from the extremely online, late Godard is a mood.

senses.d: Used to express that the speaker finds something very relatable.
ex: ⁠—I am feeling very exhausted today. ⁠—Mood.
Joon posted a video with a stray cat with the caption 'V's tweet was like #mood'.

senses.d: A verb form that depends on how its containing clause relates to the speaker’s or writer’s wish, intent, or assertion about reality.
ex: The mood most frequently encountered in English is the indicative, of which the mood in this sentence is an example.

grp.label: disposition — see also in the mood

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *lewk-der. Proto-Indo-European *lewk-to-s Proto-Germanic *leuhtaz Proto-West Germanic *leuht Old English lēoht Middle English light Middle English moonelight English moonlight The noun is derived from Middle English moonelight, monelight, mone lyght (“light of the moon; (heraldry) pattern of moons on the field of a heraldic banner”), from mon, mone (“moon”) (from Old English mōna (“moon”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon; month”)) + light (“light”) (from Old English lēoht (“light”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to see; to shine”))…

senses.d: The light reflected from the Moon, which seems to emanate from it.
ex: Meronym: moonbeam
Than Ripheus him ſelf adioynd, & myghty moſt with launce / Came Iphitus onto my ſide, by monelight met by chaunce.

senses.d: The silvery colour of the light reflected by the Moon.
Synonym of moonshine (“illegally produced or smuggled spirits”).
ex: A fast-sailing lugger will soon bring you there though, snug stowed under hatches, like a cask of moonlight.

senses.d: Chiefly in to do a moonlight: short for moonlight flit (“an act of secretly leaving premises without paying the rent, supposedly at night by the light of the Moon; hence, any act of escaping at night”).
A picture of a scene illuminated by light reflected by the Moon.
A journey made at night when the Moon is shining.
An oratorical competition; also, a participant in such a competition.
To do a moonlight flit: to secretly leave premises without paying the rent, supposedly at night by the light of the Moon.
To make a night-time attack on a tenant farmer not supporting the policies of the Irish National Land League.
To do work for pay (sometimes illegally, secretly, or without paying income tax on the earnings) which is in addition to a main job, often in the evening or at night.
To engage in an activity other than what one is known for.
Of a thing: to perform a secondary function substantially different from a supposed primary function.
ex: Some proteins have a primary function of acting as enzymes, but moonlight by carrying out secondary roles such as signal transduction or transcriptional regulation.

senses.d: Of a tenant farmer: to be attacked for not supporting the policies of the Irish National Land League.
